correctness.rationale: Exact component derivative is \(q-pq(1-q)\), bounded in absolute value by \(1+p/4\) uniformly in valuation. In the induction a tiny positive new weight preserves all old strict alternating derivative witnesses. The old mixture derivative eventually approaches zero from below, so at a later price the new high-valuation component makes the derivative positive. Just beyond the new valuation all component derivatives are negative, adding one separated maximum and one intervening minimum. Analyticity gives strictness, and normalization/continuity yield positive normalized shares and open-set stability. The four finite examples were checked with 50 exact rational Taylor-remainder interval assertions in the standalone checker; the induction is the proof for arbitrary m.

originality.rationale: The finite-mixture logit model and two-segment single-product multimodality are known. The assessed new content is an all-integer lower bound of at least m strict local maximum prices with only one product, equal price slopes, and a relatively open set of parameters for each m. An exact induction adds a new separated maximum for every segment. The relevant inspected literature documents two-segment examples, equilibrium conditions and pricing algorithms, not this all-m theorem. No claim of definitive novelty or independent priority certification is made.
residual_risks: An unlocated older theory of extrema of positive mixtures of logistic or sigmoidal price-response curves may already contain a general theorem implying this lower bound.
Not every historical preprint, appendix, or nonindexed mathematics document on finite-mixture pricing was exhaustively accessed.
An independent specialist priority assessment has not been performed.

value.rationale: A natural pricing model has an intrinsically unbounded number of local optima in only one decision variable and for one product, without heterogeneous price coefficients. This separates segmentation-induced complexity from the familiar multiple-product nonconvexity and demonstrates a reason global or multistart price optimization can matter. The parameter-open construction is structural, not a single numerical exception. It does not claim empirical difficulty, hard complexity, or an exact upper bound.
